slides.title: C-reactive protein (CRP)
slides.eyebrow: Proteins and inflammation · What it is used for · 1/2
bullets: Specimen: Venous blood (serum)  ·  Units: mg/dL

What it is used for: CRP shows how much inflammation is present in the body. It is ordered with symptoms of a bacterial infection (fever or chills, rapid heart rate, rapid breathing, nausea and vomiting), to check for a chronic inflammatory condition, to monitor for infection after surgery, to follow a condition and its treatment, and to help make treatment decisions in sepsis.
CRP rises and falls with the amount of inflammation, so a falling CRP suggests that treatment is working or that the body is healing on its own.

slides.title: C-reactive protein (CRP)
slides.eyebrow: Proteins and inflammation · What it is used for · 2/2
bullets: Physiology: CRP is made by the liver in response to inflammation. Short-lived acute inflammation helps tissues heal from injury or infection, whereas long-lasting (chronic) inflammation can damage healthy tissue; it is most often caused by autoimmune disorders, but also by repeated injury or irritation, for example from smoking.

slides.title: C-reactive protein (CRP)
slides.eyebrow: Proteins and inflammation · Interpreting the result
bullets: High: High CRP may indicate an acute or chronic condition, such as bacterial or viral infections, inflammatory bowel disease (Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis), autoimmune disorders (lupus, rheumatoid arthritis, vasculitis) or lung diseases such as asthma. Smoking and exposure to environmental toxins, such as polluted air, can also raise CRP.

High: Healthy people usually have very low CRP, and any increase may mean inflammation. Increases have also been linked to insomnia, depression, hormone therapy for menopause and obesity, and females often have slightly higher CRP than males.

slides.title: C-reactive protein (CRP)
slides.eyebrow: Proteins and inflammation · Pre-analytics and interferences
bullets: Interferences: Some medicines and supplements may affect the result; tell the provider about everything taken, including magnesium and NSAIDs such as ibuprofen and aspirin. Prescription medicines should not be stopped without talking with the provider.
Limitations: CRP shows how much inflammation there is, but not its cause or location. A diagnosis requires other test results, symptoms and medical history.
A standard CRP test should not be confused with a high-sensitivity CRP (hs-CRP) test. Both measure CRP, but hs-CRP detects very small increases and is used to estimate the risk of heart disease.

slides.title: Procalcitonin (PCT)
slides.eyebrow: Infections (serology) · What it is used for · 1/3
bullets: Specimen: Venous blood

What it is used for: Procalcitonin is mostly used in seriously ill people — usually hospitalized — when a systemic (whole-body) infection is suspected. It helps show whether bacteria or a virus is causing the infection, for example to tell bacterial from viral pneumonia: antibiotics help most bacterial infections, but not viral ones.

The test may help to diagnose or rule out a bacterial infection and/or sepsis, find out how serious sepsis is, make treatment decisions (such as the need for antibiotics), monitor how treatment is working, and diagnose kidney infection in children with urinary tract infections.

slides.title: Procalcitonin (PCT)
slides.eyebrow: Infections (serology) · What it is used for · 2/3
bullets: It is ordered with signs of sepsis or a serious bacterial infection that could become sepsis: fever or chills, clammy or sweaty skin, confusion, extreme pain, rapid heartbeat, shortness of breath, low blood pressure, reduced urine. Sepsis is a medical emergency: get help right away if an infection is not getting better or is getting worse.

slides.title: Procalcitonin (PCT)
slides.eyebrow: Infections (serology) · What it is used for · 3/3
bullets: Physiology: Normally there is very little procalcitonin in blood. In a serious bacterial infection, cells in many parts of the body release it into the bloodstream. Sepsis is the immune system’s extreme response to an infection, usually bacterial: the infection spreads into the bloodstream, triggers a chain reaction of inflammation and blood clots, and can rapidly lead to tissue damage, organ failure or death. Infections leading to sepsis most often start in the lungs, urinary tract, skin or digestive system.

slides.title: Procalcitonin (PCT)
bullets: High: High procalcitonin means that sepsis is most likely, that there may be a high risk of severe sepsis and septic shock, or a serious systemic bacterial infection that raises the risk of sepsis. The higher the level, the higher the risk of sepsis and septic shock.

High: Moderate to mildly high levels may point to an early systemic bacterial infection, kidney infection in children, or non-infectious conditions such as tissue damage from trauma, serious burns, recent surgery or a severe heart attack.

slides.title: Procalcitonin (PCT)
bullets: High: Slightly high levels mean sepsis is unlikely, but may signal a local bacterial infection (such as a urinary tract infection), an infection from another cause such as a virus, or a systemic infection that is just beginning. During treatment of a bacterial infection, falling or low procalcitonin means treatment is working.

slides.title: Procalcitonin (PCT)
bullets: Pre-analytics: No special preparation is needed; blood is drawn from a vein.

Limitations: Procalcitonin does not show which bacteria are causing an infection; other tests are needed for a full diagnosis. It does give important information about sepsis risk, so treatment can start sooner.

slides.title: Ferritin
slides.eyebrow: Iron and vitamins · What it is used for · 1/6
bullets: Specimen: Venous blood (serum)  ·  Units: ng/mL, µg/L

slides.title: Ferritin
slides.eyebrow: Iron and vitamins · What it is used for · 2/6
bullets: What it is used for: Ferritin is often ordered as part of a group of iron tests.

slides.title: Ferritin
slides.eyebrow: Iron and vitamins · What it is used for · 3/6
bullets: It helps diagnose or rule out hemochromatosis (iron overload), iron deficiency anemia, liver diseases (much of the body’s ferritin is stored in the liver), restless legs syndrome and adult Still disease; monitor chronic conditions that affect iron (cancer, kidney disease, autoimmune diseases); find low iron before symptoms in people at high risk (being underweight, heavy menstrual bleeding, pregnancy, poor absorption such as with inflammatory bowel disease or after gastrointestinal surgery); and check how well treatment is working.

slides.title: Ferritin
slides.eyebrow: Iron and vitamins · What it is used for · 4/6
bullets: Serum ferritin is currently the most efficient and cost-effective test for diagnosing iron deficiency. Because it falls during the first stage of iron depletion, it can identify low iron status before anemia develops.

slides.title: Ferritin
slides.eyebrow: Iron and vitamins · What it is used for · 5/6
bullets: Ordered with symptoms of low iron (shortness of breath, weakness, dizziness, arrhythmia, pale skin, restless legs syndrome) or high iron (weakness, joint pain, loss of interest in sex, abdominal pain, gray, metallic or bronze skin), and when other blood tests show low hematocrit or hemoglobin.
Physiology: Ferritin is a protein that binds to iron and stores it in the body. A ferritin test shows how much iron is stored in the body.

slides.title: Ferritin
slides.eyebrow: Iron and vitamins · What it is used for · 6/6
bullets: Nearly all ferritin is inside cells; a small amount circulates in the plasma. Under normal conditions serum ferritin is directly related to the amount of stored iron: 1 µg/L of serum ferritin is equivalent to about 10 mg of stored iron.

slides.title: Ferritin
slides.eyebrow: Iron and vitamins · Interpreting the result · 1/2
bullets: High: Higher than normal ferritin can be caused by too much iron in the body. Other causes include inflammation (for example, from infection or surgery), an autoimmune disorder, liver disease, cancer, obesity, alcohol use disorder and hyperthyroidism.
High: A high ferritin level is typical in people who have hemochromatosis. Ferritin tests are also used to see whether iron levels are improving with treatment.

slides.title: Ferritin
slides.eyebrow: Iron and vitamins · Interpreting the result · 2/2
bullets: Low: Lower than normal ferritin may mean iron deficiency anemia or another condition related to low iron. Without treatment, iron deficiency anemia can lead to heart problems, infections, and slow growth and brain development in children.

Low: Iron deficiency develops in stages: 1) storage iron depletion — serum ferritin and bone marrow iron decrease; 2) iron-deficient erythropoiesis — stores are depleted and transferrin saturation declines, but hemoglobin is usually normal; 3) iron deficiency anemia — hemoglobin and hematocrit fall and red cells are small with little hemoglobin (microcytic, hypochromic anemia).

slides.title: Ferritin
slides.eyebrow: Iron and vitamins · Pre-analytics and interferences · 1/3
bullets: Pre-analytics: The provider may ask you to fast for 12 hours before the test, which is usually done in the morning.

Interferences: Ferritin is an acute-phase reactant: chronic infection, inflammation or diseases that damage tissues and organs (hepatitis, cirrhosis, neoplasia, arthritis) can raise it independent of iron status. This rise can mask depleted iron stores.
Certain medicines can decrease or increase ferritin levels; an abnormal result does not always mean a condition that needs treatment.

slides.title: Ferritin
slides.eyebrow: Iron and vitamins · Pre-analytics and interferences · 2/3
bullets: WHO (2020) recommends assessing ferritin together with two acute-phase proteins, CRP and AGP, where infection or inflammation is widespread; with inflammation the iron-deficiency cut-off is raised (adults <70 µg/L, children under 5 <30 µg/L).

Limitations: Anemia of chronic disease (anemia of inflammation) can be difficult to diagnose: although low serum ferritin indicates iron deficiency, ferritin tends to be higher with infection or inflammation. In this anemia, inflammatory cytokines raise hepcidin and iron is diverted from the circulation to storage sites.

slides.title: Ferritin
slides.eyebrow: Iron and vitamins · Pre-analytics and interferences · 3/3
bullets: In the anaemia algorithm ferritin is the first test in microcytic (low MCV) anaemia: a low ferritin confirms iron deficiency; with normal or high ferritin, anaemia of chronic disease (inflammation), thalassaemia and other causes are considered. Full path: Learn → Tables and algorithms → Anaemia.

slides.title: Fibrinogen (factor I)
slides.eyebrow: Blood clotting (coagulation) · What it is used for · 1/2
bullets: Specimen: Venous blood (sodium citrate, light-blue-top tube)

What it is used for: Fibrinogen is another name for clotting factor I. The fibrinogen test helps assess the ability to form a blood clot and is ordered with other clotting tests or when PT and/or APTT results are abnormal.

Fibrinogen is one of the coagulation factor tests, which check whether a factor is too high or too low, missing or not working right. They are also used to follow people with known factor problems or taking blood thinners.

slides.title: Fibrinogen (factor I)
slides.eyebrow: Blood clotting (coagulation) · What it is used for · 2/2
bullets: Physiology: Fibrinogen is a protein important for blood clot formation (coagulation). Another protein, thrombin, removes small pieces (fibrinopeptides) from it, converting fibrinogen to fibrin, the main protein in blood clots. Fibrin proteins attach to each other, forming the stable network of the clot.
After an injury, platelets form a plug; activated fibrin, a long, thin and sticky protein, forms a mesh that holds the platelet plug in place and traps red blood cells to form the clot.

slides.title: Fibrinogen (factor I)
cols: Higher than normal clotting factor levels may mean a disorder that makes blood clot more than it should; factor levels can be high during inflammation, pregnancy or cancer.

Low or absent fibrinogen leads to bleeding. In congenital afibrinogenemia (about 1 in 1 million newborns) there is no fibrinogen and clots do not form: bleeding from the umbilical stump, nose, gums or tongue and into joints and muscles. In hypofibrinogenemia fibrinogen is decreased — the less there is, the more severe the bleeding.

slides.title: Fibrinogen (factor I)
cols: In dysfibrinogenemia fibrinogen is present at normal levels but works abnormally, which can lead to excessive bleeding or abnormal clotting (thrombosis).

slides.title: Fibrinogen (factor I)
cols: In disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), overactive clotting comes first and then uses up platelets and clotting factors, leading to bleeding. DIC is often linked to sepsis, severe injury, burns, major surgery, pregnancy problems or cancer; several blood tests and a scoring system are used for diagnosis.

slides.title: Fibrinogen (factor I)
bullets: Pre-analytics: No special preparation is needed for this test.

Per the WHO phlebotomy guidelines, coagulation tests (including prothrombin time) use a sodium citrate tube (usually light-blue top): citrate removes calcium by forming calcium salts. This tube requires a full draw and gentle inversion to mix the blood with the additive.

If a routine coagulation assay is the only test ordered, a single light-blue tube may be drawn; if contamination by tissue fluids or thromboplastins is a concern, a non-additive tube is drawn first. When several tubes are drawn, they are filled in a set order so additives are not carried between tubes.

slides.title: Fibrinogen (factor I)
bullets: Limitations: The provider may order other tests to find the cause of a clotting factor problem. Bleeding disorders caused by other conditions usually involve low levels of two or more factors, whereas inherited ones usually involve only one.

slides.title: A patient's CRP is high. What does this result tell you on its own?
options: It confirms a bacterial infection, although it cannot show where it is located
It shows that inflammation is present, but not its cause or location
It identifies which organ is inflamed and what is causing it
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct: for a diagnosis, CRP is interpreted with other tests, symptoms and medical history.

Basis: MedlinePlus: CRP results show how much inflammation there is, but not what is causing it or where it is.

slides.title: How does a standard CRP test differ from a high-sensitivity CRP (hs-CRP) test?
options: Both measure CRP, but hs-CRP detects very small increases and is used to estimate heart disease risk
hs-CRP measures a different protein, made by the heart, that signals heart disease risk
hs-CRP is the test used for treatment decisions in sepsis, because it detects smaller changes than CRP
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct: the tests measure the same protein but are used for different conditions.

Basis: MedlinePlus: CRP and hs-CRP tests both measure CRP but are used for different conditions; hs-CRP measures very tiny increases and estimates heart disease risk.

slides.title: A patient with an active infection has a normal ferritin. Does this prove iron stores are adequate?
options: No, inflammation can raise ferritin and mask low stores
Yes, a normal ferritin always proves stores are adequate
Yes, because infection only lowers ferritin
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct. That is why ferritin is interpreted with other markers during inflammation.

Basis: Ferritin is an acute-phase reactant: inflammation raises it regardless of iron status and can mask depleted stores.

slides.title: Which clotting factor number is fibrinogen?
options: Factor VIII
Factor II
Factor I
slides.explanation:

Basis: Fibrinogen is clotting factor I.

slides.title: What does fibrinogen become during clotting, and which protein does it?
options: Into fibrin, by thrombin
Into prothrombin, by hemoglobin
Into D-dimer as a clot dissolves

Basis: Thrombin removes fibrinopeptides, converting fibrinogen to fibrin.

slides.title: Acute-phase proteins?
bullets: 1. Acute-phase proteins are plasma proteins whose concentration changes in the liver under the influence of cytokines (mainly IL-6) in inflammation, infection and injury.
2. Positive reactants (increase): CRP, serum amyloid A, procalcitonin, fibrinogen, ferritin, haptoglobin, ceruloplasmin, hepcidin, α1-antitrypsin.
3. Negative reactants (decrease): albumin, prealbumin (transthyretin), transferrin, retinol-binding protein, antithrombin.

4. CRP changes quickly (rises within hours, falls quickly after the cause is removed); <3 mg/L (0.3 mg/dL) normal; very high values are more often in bacterial infection; hs-CRP – cardiovascular risk (<1, 1–3, >3 mg/L).

slides.title: Acute-phase proteins?
bullets: 5. Procalcitonin – in bacterial infection and sepsis; an aid in starting/stopping antibiotic therapy (~0.25 ng/mL in respiratory infections, ~0.5 ng/mL in sepsis; ≥80% decrease over time).
6. ESR is an indirect marker (depends on fibrinogen and immunoglobulins), changes more slowly than CRP; consider the acute-phase effect when interpreting ferritin and albumin.

slides.title: Determining CRP, RF, ASO. Clinical and diagnostic significance?
bullets: 1. CRP is an acute-phase protein; immunoturbidimetry/nephelometry (quantitative) or latex agglutination (semi-quantitative); <3 mg/L normal; rises sharply in bacterial infection; hs-CRP – cardiovascular risk.

2. Rheumatoid factor (RF) – autoantibodies to the Fc portion of IgG (mainly IgM); latex agglutination or nephelometry; occurs in rheumatoid arthritis but is not specific (other rheumatic diseases, infections, healthy elderly); anti-CCP is more specific.

slides.title: Determining CRP, RF, ASO. Clinical and diagnostic significance?
bullets: 3. ASO (antistreptolysin-O) – antibodies to streptolysin O of group A streptococcus; begin to rise ~1 week after infection, peak at 3–6 weeks; a sign of recent streptococcal infection (rheumatic fever, poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis); dynamics in paired sera are important.
4. Disadvantages of latex tests: semi-quantitative, prozone effect, subjective reading; quantitative immunoturbidimetric methods are preferred in modern practice.
5. Results are interpreted with the clinical picture: RF/ASO alone is not a diagnosis.

slides.title: Determining acute-phase proteins?
bullets: 1. Main methods: immunoturbidimetry and immunonephelometry (CRP, haptoglobin, ceruloplasmin, α1-antitrypsin, transferrin, fibrinogen antigen), immunochemiluminescence (procalcitonin, ferritin, IL-6).
2. Fibrinogen – the functional Clauss method (based on thrombin time, on a coagulometer); albumin – dye-binding methods.
3. Electrophoresis: increase of the α1 and α2 fractions (acute inflammation pattern), decrease of albumin.
4. Semi-quantitative latex agglutination (CRP) – fast, but imprecise; quantitative methods are preferred.

slides.title: Determining acute-phase proteins?
bullets: 5. Interpretation: dynamics of CRP and procalcitonin; consider the effect of the acute phase in ferritin, albumin, transferrin results.
